statement: In laboratory studies of men who already used cocaine often, smoked and injected cocaine reached the blood within seconds, and the effects they rated peaked within about 1 to 1.5 minutes and had mostly faded within 15 to 30 minutes, while cocaine was still in the blood at 90 minutes; the snorted route was not measured in the studies read. In 9 men on a residential research unit who used both injected and smoked cocaine (study conditions, not amounts to use: 16 or 32 mg injected and 25 or 50 mg smoked, each given over 15 seconds, with each route's doses in rising order about 90 minutes apart), arterial levels peaked about 15 seconds after the dose ended, at roughly ten times the later arm-vein peak (at that moment, after 32 mg injected, 2347 ng/ml in arterial against 27 ng/ml in arm-vein blood), while arm-vein levels peaked at about 4 minutes; the two approached each other within about 20 minutes, and at 90 minutes levels after the higher doses were still above those after the lower ones. Ratings of feeling stimulated, high and liking the drug peaked about 1.0 to 1.5 minutes after either route, stayed raised for about 10 minutes, were low by 15 to 30 minutes and were no longer reported at 90 minutes; blood pressure and heart rate (about 107 beats a minute after the highest doses) peaked within about 1 to 1.5 minutes. Smoked doses gave lower blood levels than injected doses (arm-vein peaks 67 and 143 against 108 and 252 ng/ml), yet peak ratings and peak systolic pressure did not differ significantly between routes in 8 men; because sham smoking itself raised blood pressure and ratings of high, and no effect was compared with placebo or sham, the study cannot show that one route gives a stronger effect for the same blood level. Of 13 men who started, 4 were discharged in the first phase, 3 for transient premature ventricular contractions (extra heartbeats; 2 of them had received only placebo injections) and 1 for chest pain after a single smoked dose, so the men analysed are those who tolerated every dose (Evans et al., 1996). In 4 men given 100 or 200 mg into a vein over 1.5 to 3 minutes after at least 48 hours without cocaine, the highest measured level was in the first arm sample, at 5 minutes, and the level then halved every 40 to 52 minutes after 100 mg and every 79 to 82 minutes after 200 mg; the paper's equations relating half-life to dose rest on five sessions with doses compared mostly between different men, and its early values lie above the assay's calibrated range (Barnett et al., 1981). For snorting, the same paper's figures of about 60% absorbed and an 8-minute absorption half-life come from refitting another laboratory's averaged curves sampled only to 90 minutes, and a 1996 narrative review describes, second-hand from studies not read here, arm-vein peaks about 30 to 40 minutes after snorting against about 5 minutes after injecting or smoking, peak felt effects within 10 to 20 minutes, and effects lasting about 60 minutes or longer after the peak, against about 30 to 45 minutes after injecting or smoking (Hatsukami & Fischman, 1996). None of the studies read tested what happens when people take more because they feel little at first. Both primary studies were small, gave doses in an order that was not randomized and studied only men who used cocaine often. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: How fast does cocaine work, and how long does it last? In a laboratory study of 9 men who often smoked and injected cocaine, smoked or injected cocaine reached the blood within seconds. The high, and a faster heartbeat and higher blood pressure, peaked after about 1 to 1.5 minutes, and the high was mostly gone within 15 to 30 minutes, although cocaine was still in the blood at 90 minutes. In another small study of 4 men, half of an injected dose left the blood in about 40 to 80 minutes, more slowly in the two sessions with the bigger dose. Snorting was not measured in these studies: an older review says, from studies we have not read, that snorted cocaine works more slowly and for longer, so little may be felt at first. None of these studies tested what happens when people then take more. These were small studies of men who used cocaine often, given set doses in a laboratory.
population: Men who used cocaine often, studied in laboratories: 9 men who used both injected and smoked cocaine, on a residential research unit (Evans et al., 1996); 4 men with frequent use given injected cocaine (Barnett et al., 1981); snorting only through a reanalysis of another laboratory's averaged data and a 1996 narrative review

comparator: Arterial against arm-vein blood drawn at the same moments; injected against smoked cocaine in the same men; lower against higher doses (placebo and sham sessions were run but not analysed)
outcome: Time course of blood cocaine levels, heart rate, blood pressure and rated effects (stimulated, high, drug liking); elimination half-life
magnitude: Evans et al. (1996), 8 to 9 men, 15-second administration: arterial peak about 15 seconds after the end of administration (after 32 mg injected, 2347 ng/ml arterial against 27 ng/ml arm-vein at that moment); arm-vein peaks at about 4 minutes, 108 and 252 ng/ml after 16 and 32 mg injected and 67 and 143 ng/ml after 25 and 50 mg smoked; arterial peaks higher, F(1,7) = 91.353, P < .0001, and earlier, F(1,7) = 52.158, P < .0002, than arm-vein peaks, with no difference in timing by route or dose; injected above smoked peaks, F(1,7) = 7.613, P < .0281. Ratings peaked at about 1.0 (high), 1.25 (liking) and 1.5 minutes (stimulated), stayed raised about 10 minutes, were low by 15 to 30 minutes and absent at 90 minutes (data not shown); heart rate peaked near 107 beats a minute at 1.45 minutes on average; systolic pressure at the first reading, about 1 minute (cuff peaks 158 and 154 mm Hg after 32 mg injected and 50 mg smoked). Barnett et al. (1981), 4 men, 100 or 200 mg into a vein over 1.5 to 3 minutes: 5-minute levels 682 to 1005 ng/ml after 100 mg and 2530 and 3868 ng/ml after 200 mg, the highest measured in each session; terminal half-lives 40.3, 47.2 and 51.5 minutes after 100 mg and 78.9 and 82.3 minutes after 200 mg (51.5 against 82.3 in the one man given both). No interval is given for any time estimate.

risk_of_bias.note: Both studies are at high risk on their study cards (RoB 2): the order of doses was not randomized (Evans et al.: rising doses within a day and the order of the two test days not reported; Barnett et al.: doses compared mostly between different men), the route was open, ratings were spoken aloud to staff, the smoked dose actually inhaled is unknown, and Barnett et al.'s early values lie above the assay's calibrated range. inconsistency.note: The two studies measured different things; where they overlap (the highest arm-vein level within about 5 minutes of an injected dose) they agree.

indirectness.note: Men only, experienced with both routes or using often; a timed 15-second smoking procedure unlike usual smoking and injections over 15 seconds to 3 minutes; laboratory doses; snorting, the most common route, only through a reanalysis of another laboratory's averaged data and a narrative review.

imprecision.note: 8 to 9 and 4 men; no interval for any time estimate; half-lives from five sessions.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive laboratory timing data start low (relation 'describes', METHODS §6.1, §6.3). Risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 take the rating below the floor: very low. Status single study: each finding rests on one primary study (Evans et al., 1996, for the timing of effects and of arterial against arm-vein levels by route; Barnett et al., 1981, for elimination after injected doses), which agree only on the early arm-vein peak after injection; the narrative review's figures for snorting are second-hand and used only to qualify. Not used, following the study cards: Barnett et al.'s general equations relating half-life and clearance to dose (five sessions, mostly between different men), its threshold in initial concentration (it mixes fitted model types) and its build-up after a repeated dose (one session in one man, outside the methods and above the calibrated range); Evans et al.'s conclusion that smoked cocaine does not reach the brain faster than injected cocaine (brain levels were not measured, and arterial samples were 15 seconds apart).

statement: In US household surveys from 2002 to 2016 (National Surveys on Drug Use and Health), among people who had first used cocaine less than 12 months before the interview, an estimated 5.0% (95% CI 4.0% to 6.3%) of those who had used only powder, and 22.2% (16.7% to 29.4%) of those who had gone on to crack, met DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence by the time they were interviewed; the estimates are summaries of seven two-year survey pairs, based on 3,488 and 275 powder-only and powder-then-crack initiates in all (9 to 96 per year-pair in the second group). Of 21 dependence-related problems asked about, the most frequent in both groups was wanting or trying to cut down or stop using cocaine (45.4%, 43.1% to 47.9%, against 58.3%, 53.0% to 64.2%) and the least frequent was continuing to use despite physical problems caused or worsened by cocaine (1.9% against 2.8%, the difference not significant); most of the other problems were more common in the group who had gone on to crack, with at least one exception and one item whose estimate the paper does not plot. The two groups are not comparable exposures: the comparison is unadjusted, the survey asks about cocaine in any form rather than which form caused a problem, and reaching crack within the same 12 months takes time and continued use, so time since first use, which is not reported for either group, and amount used may differ. The paper's authors give three readings of the difference without choosing between them: people who go on to crack may be more susceptible from the outset; some may become dependent on powder and then start crack; or something about crack smoking may raise the risk. The figures rest on self-reported diagnosis in a household and group-quarters survey (people in institutions are outside the sampling frame), without characteristics reported for either group, and the item wording sits in supplements that were not available. The 22% is not shown to be the same as the roughly 30% reported for newly started heroin use in a separate study: no test is reported and the interval stops at 29.4%. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: How quickly can dependence start after someone first uses cocaine? In US surveys, about 5 in 100 people who had started cocaine in the past year, and used only powder, met the criteria for cocaine dependence by the time they were asked. Among those who had also gone on to crack, it was about 22 in 100. The most common problem in both groups was wanting or trying to cut down or stop. This does not show that crack itself causes dependence: people who go on to crack may differ to begin with, some may already have problems with powder, and the survey did not ask which form caused a problem. The surveys relied on what people said about themselves, and most people who start cocaine do not meet the criteria within the first year.
population: People aged 12 and over in US households and non-institutional group quarters who had first used cocaine less than 12 months before interview, 2002–2016 National Surveys on Drug Use and Health: 3,488 powder-only and 275 powder-then-crack initiates in all (effective sample sizes per two-year pair 194–590 and 9–96)
exposure: Having first used cocaine within the past 12 months: powder only, or powder followed by crack (self-reported)
comparator: People who had started powder cocaine and never used crack (unadjusted comparison)
outcome: Meeting DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence, and 21 dependence-related problems, by the time of interview
magnitude: Chandra & Anthony (2020), meta-analysis summaries of seven two-year survey pairs: dependence within 1–12 months of first use 5.0% (95% CI 4.0% to 6.3%) in powder-only initiates and 22.2% (16.7% to 29.4%) in powder-then-crack initiates (the paper's Conclusions print 20% for the second). Year-pair estimates 2.9% to 7.0% and 10.3% to 30.0%, the widest interval running from 9.2% to 64.5%. Problem items: wanting or trying to cut down or stop 45.4% (43.1% to 47.9%) against 58.3% (53.0% to 64.2%), difference p < 0.05; continuing to use despite physical problems 1.9% (1.6% to 2.4%) against 2.8% (1.6% to 5.2%), p > 0.05. The study card's reading of the figure: powder-only estimates below 10% for 17 of the 20 plotted items, powder-then-crack estimates 15% or more for 14; one item about equal in the two groups and one (about 36% against 28%) higher in the powder-only group. No adjusted estimate, no absolute difference with an interval and no per-month risk are given.

statement: Crack and powder are the same drug in two forms, and the sources read describe what differs as the route each form allows, the amounts and patterns of use that go with it, and the circumstances of the people using it, rather than a property of crack itself; no source read tests crack against powder with those differences accounted for. Powder cannot be smoked because it breaks down at the temperature needed, while the base form (crack) can, so the form sets the route; once in the blood, a narrative review describes the two forms as eliminated and broken down alike, with smoked and injected cocaine reaching peak blood levels within about 5 minutes against about 30 to 40 minutes for snorting (second-hand from studies not read here; Hatsukami & Fischman, 1996). In US household surveys of 1995–1998, among 855 people who had started cocaine within the previous 0–23 months, each of seven dependence features was reported about 2 to 4 times as often by the 190 who had started crack as by the 572 who had started powder and never used crack (weighted occurrence in the past year about 18% to 32% against about 5% to 12%); the summary odds ratio across features, adjusted for sex, age, race, daily drinking, daily tobacco smoking, injecting and the number of days cocaine was used, was 1.9 (95% CI 1.4 to 2.5), and 1.6 (1.0 to 2.5) for 93 people who had started crack after two or more years of powder use; without the term for days of use the estimate was about 2.3 to 3.7, reported without intervals (Chen & Anthony, 2004). plain: Is crack more addictive or more harmful than powder cocaine? They are the same drug in two forms. Powder cannot be smoked, so the form sets how people take it, and smoking or injecting reaches the blood in minutes while snorting takes about half an hour. statement: In cross-sectional studies, people with cocaine dependence or cocaine use disorder score lower on average than comparison groups who do not use cocaine on several tests of memory, attention, stopping a started response and decision making, but the size of the difference is uncertain, the studies disagree, and none of the designs can show that cocaine caused it or that scores recover with time off cocaine. Four reviews, all rated critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2, cover overlapping literatures. A 2005 effect-size review of 15 studies (481 people who used cocaine, 586 comparison participants, 1987–2002) gives a median difference of about 0.35 standard deviations across 140 test measures, 93 of them from a single study; on the measures used in several studies the differences are smaller and mixed (Trail Making B 0.49 across 9 estimates, Trail Making A 0.19 across 10, Stroop colour-word interference −0.11 across 7), while the largest values, around 1 standard deviation, come from single small studies, the largest of them on a test the cocaine group did better on. A 2013 review pooled three to nine cross-sectional studies per outcome, dropping studies that raised heterogeneity in four of eight pools, and reported standardized differences of 0.24 to 1.22, all in the direction of poorer performance; its heterogeneity statistics are not printed. A 2026 meta-analysis of 20 studies of laboratory inhibition tasks (542 people with cocaine use disorder, 656 comparison participants) gives g = 0.65 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.03) with a 95% prediction interval of −0.95 to 2.26, significant funnel asymmetry (Egger p = .008), and two small studies whose effects (3.1 to 4.9) lie far outside the rest; without those two the first reader's recalculation gives 0.41 (0.20 to 0.62) with the asymmetry gone. A 2018 critical review of 47 studies argues the opposite reading, that the evidence does not support broad deficits, mainly because most studies did not compare performance with test norms, did not match groups on age or education and did not control for other drug use; its own table nonetheless lists poorer performance of a cocaine group in at least one area in 19 of the 21 studies with a comparison group (the first reader's count), and in the one study using age-adjusted scores the cocaine group's impairment was mild, less than 1 standard deviation below the comparison mean. Where abstinence is reported it varies from current use to about three years, and in both the 2013 and 2018 reviews a substantial minority of studies tested people within 72 hours of last use or with positive urine tests; no review could analyse whether scores differ by time since last use, and the 2026 meta-analysis, whose own criterion was at most two months, included five studies with average abstinence of 152 to 335 days. In almost every study the cocaine groups also used alcohol, cannabis or other drugs (6.7% to 100% alcohol and 12.5% to 80% cannabis across the 2026 review's tables), comparison groups often had more education and were younger, and nothing was adjusted for; the one study read in full that followed people through four weeks of enforced abstinence had no comparison group at all, and within it heavier reported drinking and heavier reported cocaine use predicted different tests (Bolla et al., 2000). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Does cocaine affect memory and thinking? On average, people with cocaine problems score somewhat lower than people who do not use cocaine on tests of memory, attention and stopping yourself. How much lower is very uncertain: reviews that put the studies together disagree, and in the newest one the range of likely results runs from a large gap to no gap at all. Everyone was tested once, after they had been using, so the tests cannot show that cocaine caused the difference. In most studies the people who used cocaine also drank or used other drugs, and the comparison groups often had more schooling. Some people were tested within three days of last use. Most studies did not compare scores with the usual range for people of the same age and schooling, and one review says this makes the picture of broad problems inaccurate. No study we read followed people long enough, with a comparison group, to show whether scores get better after stopping.

inconsistency.note: I² 83.6% with a prediction interval from −0.95 to 2.26 in the newest meta-analysis; the most-used tests in the 2005 review range from −0.11 to 0.49 with between-study spreads larger than the means; the 2013 and 2018 reviews read largely overlapping evidence in opposite directions.

indirectness.note: Second-hand throughout: every anchor is a review's account of primary studies not read here (METHODS §6.3), except one primary study that has no comparison group. imprecision.note: The pooled estimates rest on hundreds of people and have usable intervals; imprecision is not downgraded again, since the wide prediction interval is rated under inconsistency.

publication_bias.note: Significant funnel asymmetry in the 2026 meta-analysis (Egger p = .008) with no adjusted estimate, driven by two small studies with very large effects; the 2005 and 2013 reviews did not assess publication bias; the 2018 review notes in passing that selecting significant comparisons overstates estimates.

grade.reasoning: Cross-sectional evidence starts low. Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1, indirectness −1 and publication bias −1 take it well below the floor: very low. Status mixed: the direction is reported consistently, but the size is not, the reviews of the same literature reach opposite conclusions about whether it amounts to impairment, and the newest pooled estimate halves when two outlying small studies are removed. The four reviews are not independent: the 2013 review was written to follow on from the 2005 one, the 2018 review tabulates studies also covered by the 2013 one, and the 2026 meta-analysis covers the same literature without citing any of them; they are counted once. statement: In the nine placebo-controlled randomized trials published up to 2006 and pooled in one review (640 patients with cocaine dependence, 344 given a stimulant medicine and 296 placebo, all with psychological treatment as well), stimulant medicines did not detectably reduce how many people dropped out (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.10, with no difference for any single medicine) or the proportion of urine samples positive for a cocaine breakdown product in the trials that reported it (0.94, 0.84 to 1.05 across six trials; 0.84, 0.67 to 1.04 leaving out bupropion). Only an exploratory analysis, which filled in cocaine use for three further trials as the average of their starting and final values and used per-protocol rather than all-randomized data for two dexamphetamine trials, found fewer positive samples with dexamphetamine (0.73, 0.60 to 0.90) and with the medicines pooled (0.87, 0.77 to 0.99); that signal rests on filled-in outcomes, on two trials by one research group, and in part on one treatment arm in which 42 of 46 people dropped out, and the review's own authors call per-protocol bias unlikely without testing it. Modafinil's estimate in the main analysis was not significant (0.73, 0.50 to 1.04). More people stopped taking a stimulant than placebo because of unwanted effects (15 of 344, 4.4%, against 4 of 296, 1.3%; p = 0.03), the most common being sleeping problems, anxiety and jitteriness; the review's statement that no serious unwanted effect was reported has no counterpart in its results, which describe the information on unwanted effects as too limited for conclusions, and several trials did not say how they were assessed. The trials were small (30 to 149 patients, 42 to 182 days), nearly 9 in 10 participants were men, about half were also dependent on opioids and most smoked or injected cocaine, and the review calculates that 144 to 584 patients per arm would have been needed to detect a difference, more than any trial had; its own confidence was rated critically low, and the two headline figures printed in its abstract appear nowhere in its results. Craving could not be pooled. This is the evidence up to 2006 only: later reviews of these medicines, including modafinil and methylphenidate, have not been read. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do stimulant medicines help people stop using cocaine? In nine trials up to 2006, with 640 people who all also had talking therapy, people given a stimulant medicine were no more likely to stay in treatment, and no less likely to have urine tests positive for cocaine, than people given a dummy pill. One extra analysis, which filled in missing results and left out people who stopped taking the medicine, did find fewer positive tests with dexamphetamine, but that result is not reliable. More people stopped the medicine because of unwanted effects, such as trouble sleeping, anxiety and jitteriness: about 4 in 100 against about 1 in 100 on the dummy pill. The trials were small, most of the people were men, and about half also had problems with opioids. Newer reviews of these medicines have not been read yet.

risk_of_bias.note: Randomized and double-blind, but the review's confidence is AMSTAR 2 critically low on its study card: no protocol, no list of excluded trials, a reporting-quality scale instead of a risk-of-bias assessment, an outcome that treats each group's proportion of positive urine samples as if it were a proportion of patients, per-protocol data pooled with all-randomized data, about 48% dropout in both arms and no examination of unblinding by the medicines' own effects.

inconsistency.note: I² 0% for dropout and consistent null estimates across five medicines in the main analysis; the only estimate pointing to benefit comes from the exploratory analysis with imputed outcomes, which the claim reports as such.

indirectness.note: Not downgraded: the claim is worded for the people, medicines, comparison and outcomes of these trials, and says in its population that 11.9% were women, about half were also opioid-dependent and most smoked or injected cocaine, that every trial added psychological treatment and that follow-up ran to at most 182 days. The handling of the cocaine-use outcome (each group's proportion of positive urine samples entered as if it were a proportion of patients, and per-protocol data pooled with all-randomized data) is rated once, under risk of bias, not twice (METHODS §6.3). That the evidence stops in 2006 is a matter of currency, flagged in the claim and in its verification note rather than rated here.

imprecision.note: 640 patients in all against the review's own estimate of 144 to 584 per arm; the intervals around the null estimates (0.85 to 1.10 for dropout, 0.84 to 1.05 for cocaine use, 0.67 to 1.04 without bupropion) still allow reductions of up to about a third in cocaine-positive samples, so this is a failure to detect a difference, not a demonstration that none exists.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review; its searches covered three databases with contact with first authors, and eight of nine trials were publicly funded.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high. Risk of bias −1 (the review's handling of the cocaine-use outcome and of per-protocol data, about 48% dropout in both arms, and its critically low AMSTAR 2 confidence) and imprecision −1 (intervals that still allow a clinically meaningful reduction, against the review's own estimate that 144 to 584 patients per arm would be needed) give low certainty; indirectness is not downgraded, because the claim is worded for the people and outcomes of these trials and the outcome's handling is already counted under risk of bias. Worded as no detectable difference, not as equivalence, as METHODS §6.3 requires: the interval does not exclude a worthwhile benefit. Status replicated: nine independent trials of five medicines point the same way on dropout and on the main cocaine-use outcome. Not used, following the study card: the exploratory dexamphetamine and pooled estimates as evidence of efficacy, the abstract's headline figures, and its statement that no serious unwanted effect occurred.
